claims.text: A conventional powder-metallurgy W–Cu composite has a random microstructure with separate tungsten and copper phases.
A graphene-nanoplatelet loading of approximately 1–5 wt% is a suitably low addition for W–Cu.
Controlled stirring, tape casting, or lamination can preferentially align graphene nanoplatelets along W–Cu phase boundaries.
High heat flux, high working temperatures, and neutron or charged-particle irradiation are representative conditions for fusion-reactor joints and related applications.
Aligned graphene nanoplatelets will form percolating networks that bridge tungsten and copper domains at key interfaces.
Graphene has ultrahigh in-plane thermal conductivity.
Aligned graphene pathways can bypass thermal interfacial resistance between tungsten and copper.
Graphene has excellent mechanical strength.
Graphene has intrinsic irradiation tolerance.
Graphene reinforcement will help preserve W–Cu structural integrity during thermal cycling.
Graphene reinforcement will help preserve W–Cu structural integrity during radiation exposure.
The graphene-modified W–Cu composite will have higher effective thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable graphene-free W–Cu composite.
The graphene-modified composite will maintain or improve mechanical durability relative to the graphene-free W–Cu control.
The graphene-modified composite will maintain or improve irradiation resistance relative to the graphene-free W–Cu control.
Keeping graphene at approximately 1–5 wt% will avoid disrupting metallic connectivity in W–Cu.
Extreme graphene loadings may cause deleterious effects in W–Cu.
Interfacial reactions involving graphene may cause deleterious effects in W–Cu.
The optimal graphene loading for alignment without compromising metal–metal bonding is not established.
The optimal processing method for aligning graphene without compromising metal–metal bonding is not established.
The long-term irradiation behavior of graphene-containing W–Cu interfaces under reactor conditions requires further study.
